explanations.explanation: This feature detects the start of a new block or header—i.e. the first token after a paragraph/line break (beginning of a post, heading, list item, etc.).

This neuron fires on subword tokens that are standalone uppercase initials of capitalized words appearing mid‐sentence or in titles (e.g. the “G” of Grip, the “W” of Wiring, the “T” of Tire, the “F” of Fertel, etc.), effectively marking non–sentence‐initial word‐starts in product names, headings, dates, personal names, resolutions, lists, and similar contexts.

This neuron is basically a “subword‐prefix” detector.  It spikes on those short BPE pieces that kick off longer tokens—whether that’s the double‐prime inch mark (″) after “22″,” the first fragment of a hyphenated product name (“Go”-ose, “Cap”-ella), a mid-word medical stem (“ocol” in enterocolitis), single-letter prefixes (“v” in vintage) or other initial subword chunks in titles, model numbers, dates, etc.
This neuron is a detector for the “.” (full-stop) token, i.e. end-of-unit/sentence punctuation (including sentence-final stops and dots in abbreviations).
This neuron fires on the “head” of TitleCase/CamelCase tokens—i.e. the initial uppercase‐to‐lowercase (or digit) subword that marks the start of proper names, acronyms and brand/ID strings.
This feature is a detector for full‐stop punctuation as a strong boundary marker—i.e. the period that ends sentences (or appears in common abbreviations/titles).

explanations.explanation: This feature fires on the sentence-final punctuation of short, title-like or slogan-style opening lines in marketing or informational copy—i.e. it marks the boundary between a standalone headline/tagline and the following body text.
This feature detects the closing punctuation that marks the end of a standalone title or headline, signalling a boundary after a heading-style phrase.

This neuron is a simple “block‐boundary” detector: it spikes on the opening word of a list or headline (e.g. “More”, “This”, “Amazing”) and again on the period that ends that first summary sentence. In effect it marks the start and end of a bullet‐item or title/teaser line.

This neuron fires on the final “.” token that terminates a heading or title snippet—e.g. the end-of-title punctuation in product listings, article headlines, download links, etc. It effectively marks the boundary where a web page’s headline or item title finishes.
